Context¶

The number of restaurants in New York is increasing day by day. Lots of students and busy professionals rely on those restaurants due to their hectic lifestyles. Online food delivery service is a great option for them. It provides them with good food from their favorite restaurants. A food aggregator company FoodHub offers access to multiple restaurants through a single smartphone app.

The app allows restaurants to receive a direct online order from a customer. The app assigns a delivery person from the company to pick up the order after it is confirmed by the restaurant. The delivery person then uses the map to reach the restaurant and waits for the food package. Once the food package is handed over to the delivery person, he/she confirms the pick-up in the app and travels to the customer's location to deliver the food. The delivery person confirms the drop-off in the app after delivering the food package to the customer. The customer can rate the order in the app. The food aggregator earns money by collecting a fixed margin on the delivery order from the restaurants.

Objective¶

The food aggregator company has stored the data of the different orders made by the registered customers in their online portal. They want to analyze the data to get a fair idea about the demand of different restaurants which will help them in enhancing their customer experience. Suppose you are hired as a Data Scientist in this company and the Data Science team has shared some of the key questions that need to be answered. Perform the data analysis to find answers to these questions that will help the company improve its business.

Data Description¶

The data includes various information related to a food order. A detailed data dictionary is provided below.

Data Dictionary¶

  • order_id: Unique ID of the order
  • customer_id: ID of the customer who ordered the food
  • restaurant_name: Name of the restaurant
  • cuisine_type: Cuisine ordered by the customer
  • cost_of_the_order: Cost of the order
  • day_of_the_week: Indicates whether the order is placed on a weekday or weekend (The weekday is from Monday to Friday and the weekend is Saturday and Sunday)
  • rating: Rating given by the customer out of 5
  • food_preparation_time: Time (in minutes) taken by the restaurant to prepare the food. This is calculated by taking the difference between the timestamps of the restaurant's order confirmation and the delivery person's pick-up confirmation.
  • delivery_time: Time (in minutes) taken by the delivery person to deliver the food package. This is calculated by taking the difference between the timestamps of the delivery person's pick-up confirmation and drop-off information

Objective & Deliverables¶

Provide an analysis of the data provided for the company Foodhub. Understand the data, and provide business recommendations that can improve their business.

Cleaning or correcting data¶

We need to replace the entries in the 'rating' variable that are not numerical values. After converting the objects to nan (not a number), we can either impute of drop them.

At the outset, I believe it is best to drop these values. As the ratings are very "human" generated, and thought they can impacted by, or be correlated, with some of our other variables, they are likely eqgually, or more impacted by other factors, that we currently do not have data on, like food quality, speed to reply to queries, etc.. Hence, if we try to impute them purely from delivert time, cost of the other, or food prep time, we risk imbuding our data with errors.

Replacing the "Not given" values in the 'rating' variable with nan.

In [13]:
# Replace 'Not given' with NaN in the 'rating' column
df['rating'] = df['rating'].replace('Not given', np.nan)

# Convert the 'rating' column to numeric, coercing errors will turn non-numeric values (if any) into NaN
df['rating'] = pd.to_numeric(df['rating'], errors='coerce')

# Display the first few rows and info again to verify the changes
display(df.head())
display(df.info())

None

We can now see that we successfully converted the 'rating' variable to a float, and that it displays NaN instead of "Not given".

I believe float is good Dtype here, as we should have the rating as an average of all the ratings given for each restaurant.

Furthermore, we can now see that the non-null count is 1162. 1162 entries have data, and 1898-1162=736 or 38.78% have no ratings. This is a significant amount.

This could be because the restaurant have not had enough sales where people have given ratings. I assume that all restaurants have had historical orders on the app, though we can also assume that not all orders will capture a successful rating submission

Eventhough the number of null values is high, I believe any attempt to impute the number will skew our analysis, and therefore I will drop the value from the analysis.

Subconclusion of Understanding the Structure of the Data¶

  1. How many rows and columns are present in the data?

1898 rows, and 9 columns

  1. What are the datatypes of the different columns in the dataset?

After cleaning: order_id: int64
customer_id: int64
restaurant_name: object cuisine_type: object cost_of_the_order: float64 day_of_the_week: object rating: float64 food_preparation_time: int64
delivery_time: int64

  1. Are there any missing values in the data?

No Null values were found, though in the rating variable several values were "Not given" thus, not a real rating, and have been corrected for the analysis.

  1. Check the statistical summary of the data. What is the minimum, average, and maximum time it takes for food to be prepared once an order is placed?

Min: 20 min Mean: 27.4 min Max: 35

  1. How many orders are not rated?

736 entries in the 'rating' variable is missing, and have been converted to NaN (Not a Number), this is 38.78%.

I do not see a reliable way to impute the missing values, and recommend we drop them, to not contaminate the analysis with bias in the analsysis.

# Calculate the number of ratings each restaurant received
rating_counts = df_cleaned['restaurant_name'].value_counts()

# Filter for restaurants with more than 3 ratings
restaurants_with_enough_ratings = rating_counts[rating_counts > 3].index

# Filter the df_cleaned DataFrame to include only these restaurants
df_filtered_by_ratings = df_cleaned[df_cleaned['restaurant_name'].isin(restaurants_with_enough_ratings)]

# Calculate the average rating for these filtered restaurants
average_ratings_filtered = df_filtered_by_ratings.groupby('restaurant_name')['rating'].mean().sort_values(ascending=False)

print("Average customer rating per restaurant (top 10, with >3 ratings):")
print(average_ratings_filtered.head(10))

Restaurants for Promotional Offer¶

In [50]:
# 1. Filter restaurants with rating count > 50
restaurants_high_count = rating_counts[rating_counts > 50].index

# 2. Filter restaurants with average rating > 4
restaurants_high_avg_rating = average_ratings[average_ratings > 4].index

# 3. Find the restaurants that satisfy both conditions
qualified_restaurants = list(set(restaurants_high_count) & set(restaurants_high_avg_rating))

# 4. Display the results with their average ratings and rating counts
print("Restaurants qualifying for the promotional:")
for restaurant in qualified_restaurants:
    avg_rating = average_ratings[restaurant]
    count_rating = rating_counts[restaurant]
    print(f"- {restaurant}: Average Rating = {avg_rating:.2f}, Rating Count = {count_rating}")

Revenue Generated¶

In [51]:
# Function to calculate commission based on order cost
def calculate_commission(cost):
    if cost > 20:
        return cost * 0.25
    elif cost > 5:
        return cost * 0.15
    else:
        return 0  # No commission for orders <= 5 dollars

# Apply the function to create a new 'commission' column
df['commission'] = df['cost_of_the_order'].apply(calculate_commission)

# Calculate the net revenue (sum of all commissions)
net_revenue = df['commission'].sum()

print(f"The net revenue generated by the company across all orders is: ${net_revenue:.2f}")

Conclusion and Recommendations¶

Conclusions:¶

  1. Dominance of Key Restaurants: A small number of restaurants, particularly Shake Shack, drive a significant portion of both order volume (over 11.5% of total orders) and revenue (over 11% of total commission). The top 5 restaurants collectively contribute to a substantial 33% of the total revenue.
  2. High Weekend Activity: Weekends account for a disproportionately high number of orders (over 70%), with 'American' cuisine being the most popular. This indicates strong weekend demand but also potential for growth during weekdays.
  3. Moderate Order Costs: Nearly 30% of orders are above $20, contributing significantly to the company's commission-based revenue.
  4. Delivery Time Variances: I dont see this as a concern at the moment. There is not indication this is impacting the users, their experience, ratings, or stickiness of the product.
  5. Operational Efficiency on Weekdays: Mean delivery times are noticeably slower on weekdays (28.34 minutes) compared to weekends (22.47 minutes), suggesting potential logistical or staffing differences. This could be an impact on the lower activity during the weekdays, though I have no data to support this.

Recommendations:¶

  1. Strategic Restaurant Partnerships & Diversification:
    • Nurture Top Performers: Deepen relationships with top restaurants like Shake Shack, The Meatball Shop, Blue Ribbon Sushi, and Blue Ribbon Fried Chicken. Understand their operational efficiencies and customer appeal to replicate success where possible.
    • Revenue Growth Focus: Actively promote restaurants with high average commission per order (e.g., Kambi Ramen House, Emporio, Bhatti Indian Grill) to increase their order volume and diversify the revenue stream, reducing over-reliance on a few dominant partners.
  2. Optimize Weekday Engagement & Operations:
    • Targeted Weekday Promotions: Implement marketing campaigns and special offers (e.g., discounts on specific cuisines, free delivery) during weekdays to incentivize more orders and balance demand throughout the week.
    • Improve Weekday Delivery Efficiency: Investigate the reasons for slower weekday delivery times. This could involve optimizing driver allocation, route planning, or incentivizing faster deliveries during non-peak times.
  3. Leverage Promotional Offers Strategically:
    • Utilize the identified restaurants with high ratings and sufficient order volume (Blue Ribbon Fried Chicken, Blue Ribbon Sushi, Shake Shack, The Meatball Shop) for advertisements and promotions, as they already demonstrate customer satisfaction.
  4. Strengthen Customer Loyalty Programs:
    • Go beyond one-off vouchers for top customers. Develop a tiered loyalty program with escalating benefits (e.g., exclusive discounts, priority delivery, birthday perks) to further engage and retain highly frequent users.
    • Learn from key players in the market, Uber, Rappi, Amazon, and offer additional benefits to the "prime" or "Membership" users.

Further Analysis:¶

  1. Geospatial Analysis: Incorporate location data for restaurants and customers to analyze demand hotspots, optimize delivery zones, and assess service coverage. This would help identify areas for expansion or where delivery times could be improved.
  2. Time-of-Day Analysis: Investigate order patterns and delivery times across different hours of the day (e.g., lunch vs. dinner rush) to refine operational strategies and resource allocation.
  3. Feedback Loop Enhancement: Collect more detailed feedback, including reasons for complaints, rejections, or returned items, to identify specific areas for improvement in food quality, order accuracy, and service.
  4. Correlation with External Factors: Explore the impact of external factors like weather, local events, or competitor promotions on order volume and delivery times.

Notes and Comments¶

Ideas, or thoughts, I'd like to investigate, or explore more next time.

  1. Looking at restaurants with higher orders, and comparing that to higher price.
  2. Does busyness of the restaurant ie number of orders, impact delivery time, preparation time, or ratings?
  3. Compare number of orders per cuisine with ratings per cuisine

Appendix¶

To explore more restaurants beyond the top 5, we can define a variable num_restaurants_to_display to control how many of the top restaurants are shown. You can change this number (e.g., 25, 60) or specify a percentage (e.g., 10%) to see the corresponding top restaurants.

    count = int(len(restaurant_order_counts) * percentage)
